channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Cormac McCarthy Library Database
item.description: It would take way too long to explain how I found this: From the About page: “The Cormac McCarthy Library Database includes individual pages for each book in McCarthy’s library. The books were cataloged using Libib, a library management platform that uploads metadata about a book when that information is available, including author, title, publication information, identification numbers like ISBNs and Library of Congress numbers (LCCNs), a short description, and a cover image.” There are about 20,000 books in the database.

item.title: Explore Over 40 Years of Student Literary Works and Art in Latest DigitalNC Batch
item.description: DigitalNC: “Thanks to our partner, St. Andrews University, a batch containing 56 literary and art publication issues are now available on DigitalNC. These publications hail from both St. Andrews University as well as Sandhills Community College. Issues in this batch date all the way back to 1970 to 2014. They feature art, poems, stories, and other literary works written and created by students at the respective schools.”

item.title: How viewers followed the U.S. midterm elections on YouTube
item.description: YouTube Blog: “On Election Day alone, over 35 million U.S. viewers watched election-related content on the platform. Globally, over 40 million viewers watched livestreams related to the U.S. midterm elections, with viewership peaking at over 3 million concurrent viewers at 10:19 p.m. ET.”

item.title: In Ukraine, occupiers have damaged 2,185 cultural heritage sites—Ministry of Culture
item.description: UA News: “The Ministry of Culture of Ukraine reported that, as of the end of October, 2,185 cultural heritage sites and 2,686 cultural institutions had been damaged in Ukraine as a result of Russia’s armed aggression. According to the ministry, 48 monuments have been completely destroyed; specifically, 199 of the damaged sites are of national significance, 1,781 are of local significance, and 205 have only recently been identified.”

item.title: What Is ‘Woke 3’? The Slang Term And Viral Memes Reacting To The 2026 U.S. Midterm Elections ‘Blue Sweep’ Explained
item.description: Know Your Meme: “The Democrats have officially won the House and Senate in the U.S. in what’s being called a ‘Bluenami,’ and now social media users are ushering in the era of ‘Woke 3.’ Memes about Woke 3 are going viral everywhere, from TikTok to X / Twitter, but some people are wondering when we even went through ‘Woke 2.’ So, what is the Woke 3 slang and meme all about, and why is it going viral right now? Here’s what you need to know.”

item.title: Google Glitch Served ‘Sensitive Ads’ To Users
item.description: MediaPost: “A software error in Google’s ad platform that persisted for nearly three years resulted in ‘sensitive ads’ being served to some users, according to a new court filing by Google in a long-running privacy lawsuit.”

item.title: UCL lecturer and far-right influencer arrested following fight in front of university campus
item.description: The Tab: UCL in this case is University College London. “A fight between a UCL lecturer and a far-right influencer resulted in both participants being arrested on suspicion of affray. The altercation between lecturer Dr. Toyin Agbetu and far-right influencer, Thomas Moffitt, took place at around 12.42pm on Wednesday, just outside of the Uni’s Student Centre.”

item.title: At least 10 local governments have moved to drop Flock’s surveillance cameras since summer
item.description: TechCrunch: “At least 10 local governments and police departments have moved since this summer to curb, restrict, or end their use of Flock Safety technology as concerns about mass surveillance and data privacy continue to grow. The backlash is part of a broader pushback against the rapid adoption of advanced AI technology, including the data center buildout, facial recognition, and other uses of AI.”

item.title: Photo Location Data on a Blog: Which Platforms Strip GPS on Upload, and Where the Original Still Has It
item.description: JustBlogged Blog: “A photo taken on a phone with location access turned on usually carries the GPS coordinates of where it was taken, stored in the file’s EXIF block. Whether those coordinates reach your readers depends on what your blogging platform does to the file at upload, and on which copy of the file it serves. As of October 8, 2026, the answer differs a lot by platform.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: New TiRADE database logs every tariff rate Trump has announced
item.description: Brown Daily Herald: “A new database from Brown’s Global Linkages Lab records every tariff rate President Donald Trump has ‘threatened, announced or implemented’ since taking office. The database — titled Tariff Rates in Announcements, Declarations and Events — tracks tariffs that were announced in speeches, social media posts, executive orders or White House Statements, among other sources. Although most of the tariffs never took effect, researchers say that the markets reacted anyway.”

item.title: UKRI launches faster, easier-to-use Gateway to Research
item.description: UK Research and Innovation: “A new version of Gateway to Research (GtR), UK Research and Innovation’s (UKRI) free public database of the research and innovation it funds, is now live. … GtR lets anyone search projects funded by UKRI’s research councils and Innovate UK. It shows who is involved, how much funding was awarded and what each project has produced.”

item.title: New European database to support environmental risk assessment of human pharmaceuticals
item.description: Radboud University: “The PREMIER project, a public-private European consortium of research organisations (like Radboud University) and international pharmaceutical companies supported by the Innovative Medicines Initiative (IMI), has launched a new database to support the environmental risk assessment (ERA) of human pharmaceuticals. This data is publicly accessible, free of charge.”

item.title: X says police order demanding removal of Indian free-speech groups’ accounts was fake
item.description: Reuters: “Police orders asking X to block online accounts of two of India’s most prominent free speech groups were fake, the social media company told an Indian court on Friday, days after the purported content removal requests sparked a public outcry.”

item.title: Meta puts controversial web scraping policy changes on hold indefinitely
item.description: Mashable: “These changes, which Nieman Lab originally reported on in October, would have allowed the use of web scrapers to collect material from websites associated with Meta business accounts, including those of journalistic organizations. Originally, these changes were set to go into effect on Oct. 30, before controversy prompted Meta to delay to Nov. 20. Now, Meta has confirmed that the changes will be delayed indefinitely.”

item.title: Poynter’s MediaWise launches global initiative pairing newsrooms with independent creators
item.description: Poynter: “Around the world, more than a quarter of people now get at least some of their information from creators or influencers focused on current events. As more audiences turn to them alongside traditional news organizations, newsrooms and creators are increasingly reaching the same people. To explore how they can work together, Poynter’s MediaWise, in partnership with Microsoft, announced the Creator + Newsroom Studio at Media Party in Buenos Aires, Argentina.”

item.title: Piaggio Pledges To Protect and Promote Archives
item.description: AIN: “Piaggio Aerospace has signed a five-year agreement with Italy’s Ministry of Culture this month to help preserve the company’s historical archive material. Inked in Rome with the General Directorate of Archives, the agreement will support the preservation and digitalization of content, as well as promote the archive to the public.”

item.title: Sweden Returns Benin Bronze Trove to Nigeria, Indigenous Remains to Bolivia
item.description: ARTnews: “Nigerian media report that the artworks are expected to be received by a delegation from the Benin Palace in Lagos today, a development that Oba Ewuare II, the monarch of Benin, described as years in the making. Since ascending to the throne, Ewuare has advocated fiercely for the return of bronze sculptures, ceremonial objects, and ivory carvings—collectively known as the Benin Bronzes—from museum and private collections worldwide, with considerable success.”

item.title: How Online Maps Lay Bare the US Military Bases Targeted by Iran
item.description: Bellingcat: “Google Maps and other online mapping services contain dozens of labels identifying facilities including headquarters, accommodation, gyms and fuel points. Publicly available photographs and videos, including material published by the US military, provide further details about how these facilities are used.”

item.title: Parents sue Google after 13-year-old allegedly used AI to plan suicide
item.description: Euronews: “The girl, identified as Emma, was unable to access Google’s Gemini app or OpenAI’s ChatGPT, as both had been blocked by her school. However, she could still access Google’s search engine, which includes AI-powered features. Despite having ‘no history’ of mental illness, Emma began a ‘quiet spiral into a severe psychological crisis’ within months of using the search engine, according to the complaint.”

item.title: Explore the new Species Profile and Threats Database
item.description: Government of Australia: “A new Species Profile and Threats Database (SPRAT) beta website is now available. SPRAT provides trusted information on Australia’s plants, animals and ecosystems protected under the EPBC Act 1999. Explore the SPRAT beta website. Try the new features and let us know how we can continue to improve it.”

item.title: Reviving Google Cardboard, Without Google Or Cardboard
item.description: Hackaday: “Remember Google Cardboard? The late, unlamented practice of strapping a phone to your face so you could get motion sickness in a virtual environment? [brenpoly] wants you to reconsider, because in the years since Google pulled the plug on mobile VR, phones have gotten really, really good and he’s got a project called CardboardXR on GitHub that the project video enbedded below bills as ‘A 5$ Apple Vision Pro’.” Here’s a shaker of salt to take that quote with. Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Website Selling ‘AI Slop Audiobooks’ Shuts Down Following Fierce Backlash From Authors
item.description: Gizmodo: “Last week, fan fiction aficionados around the world were dismayed to discover that the popular website Archive of Our Own (AO3), which hosts just shy of nineteen million fanfic works, had gone dark. In a statement, the Organization for Transformative Works, the nonprofit which runs AO3, said the site had to be pulled offline due to a ‘security incident’ and that it could remain down for up to a month. Then AI swooped in and saved the day. And by ‘save the day’ we mean made everything a whole lot worse.”

item.title: Google refused 54K-name petition, say campaigners
item.description: BBC: “Protesters claim Google’s headquarters in London refused a petition of 54,000 signatories worried about the environmental impact of an Essex development. The tech giant plans to build four data centre buildings, covering 130,500 sqm, and an office building on the former Arena Essex Raceway near Purfleet which closed in 2018.”

item.title: Regulators Reject Duke’s Data Center Rate Structure
item.description: News Service Florida: “Florida utility regulators rejected Duke Energy Florida’s proposal to meet the requirements of a new state law intended to shield ratepayers from the costs of data centers.”

item.title: OpenAI Wants to Change the Name of Data Centers to the Stupidest Thing You’ve Ever Heard in Your Life
item.description: Futurism: “According to [Axios], OpenAI is gearing up to ‘unleash a policy and PR blitz’ as soon as the midterm elections conclude by rebranding data centers with a ludicrously euphemistic moniker: ‘AI compute campuses.'”

item.title: Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents
item.description: CNBC: “The next time someone’s supercharged AI agent attempts to make a phone call to negotiate a cable bill, it could be an actual human who haggles with customer service rather than the software. That’s because AI agents, powered by the bleeding-edge foundation models developed by companies like Meta and OpenAI, still can’t reliably take actions across the web, particularly those involving phone calls.”

item.title: “No human at the helm”: Delaware plan would let AI agents run entire businesses
item.description: Ars Technica: “A Delaware proposal to let companies be operated by AI agents would help the firms’ human owners evade legal responsibility for reckless and harmful actions taken by the AI, US Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) told Delaware Governor Matt Meyer in a letter yesterday.”

item.title: Connect ChatGPT or Claude to Your WordPress.com Sites, Free Through November
item.description: WordPress: “Connecting your WordPress.com site to an AI has been possible for a while, but full access came with a paid plan. Now it’s open to free sites too for a limited time, through November. That means you can connect to the WordPress ChatGPT plugin or WordPress Claude connector once, then let your AI upload a post, clear out comments, or tell you what needs attention across all your sites.”

item.title: Prompting Action: NC State AI Hub Hosts First Campus Gathering
item.description: North Carolina State University: “On Nov. 2, university leaders, faculty, staff and students were invited to discuss those topics and more at the first meeting of the NC State AI Hub. The new hub is a universitywide initiative that builds on the university’s existing strengths and facilitates interdisciplinary connection and collaboration around the use of AI. It is also intended to identify common AI-related needs across the university and to help determine areas to invest in that will deliver the greatest benefit.”

item.title: Schnell’s resignation prompts conversation on appropriate consequences for AI use
item.description: The Dartmouth: “Former Provost Santiago Schnell’s resignation over his use of artificial intelligence in published writing has prompted a national conversation around AI use and disclosure. College President Sian Leah Beilock announced Schnell’s resignation as provost and departure from Dartmouth in an Oct. 28 email to campus. In the same email, Beilock shared a report from an independent, faculty-led committee, which found that Schnell ‘used AI to meaningfully alter his writing’ and ‘failed to disclose his use of AI’ in two op-eds and two academic articles submitted to publications with AI use policies.”

item.title: Google expands AI Search ads globally as core ad growth slows
item.description: TechCrunch: “Google is bringing ads in its AI-powered Search experiences to international markets, betting that generative AI can open up new revenue opportunities even as growth in its core search advertising business slows.”

item.title: In San Francisco’s A.I. Boom, a First Date Has Become an Interview
item.description: New York Times: “San Francisco’s A.I. boom has drawn a wave of young ambitious people who are now reshaping the city’s dating life. Start-up founders and engineers are dating less because they are working more as they try to build A.I. products and establish their fortunes, many said. So when they date, they bring a high-stakes mind-set to it, which means a first coffee can feel like a final-round interview.”

item.title: OpenAI employees warned about operational security lapses for years, sources say
item.description: Reuters: “Even before OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022, some company staffers raised concerns internally about its security practices, according to five people familiar with the matter. Employees shared their concerns with top OpenAI leaders and the board of directors, the people said, adding that some staffers came away from those interactions concluding that management was more ‌focused on keeping pace with competitors like Google and Anthropic than on security.”

item.title: 3 charged in scheme to use AI to impersonate CEOs and attorneys to steal $129 million
item.description: Associated Press: “Three people accused of using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million have been indicted on charges of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, prosecutors said Thursday. Over more than a year and a half, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, targeted thousands of companies across the world in their AI scheme, according to the indictment filed in a U.S. District Court in New York.”

item.title: When social media no longer needs people, what does the ‘social’ part mean?
item.description: The Conversation: “The social media we know was once easy to define. Platforms such as Facebook or X were designed to mediate human relationships at scale: sharing stories, forming communities, debating ideas, and increasingly, monetising attention. However flawed these platforms became, they were built on one core assumption: people interacting with people. But that assumption is currently being tested.”

item.title: New Jersey is gambling on AI: Will taxpayers roll snake eyes on CoreWeave?
item.description: Jersey Vindicator: “CoreWeave is building a $1.8 billion data center at the former Merck campus in Kenilworth. In return, New Jersey approved $250 million in tax credits, $50 million a year for five years, for a facility expected to create just 143 permanent jobs. That works out to approximately $1.75 million in taxpayer subsidies per job.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: After Police Removal, an Archive Preserves the Memory of an LA Encampment
item.description: Shelterforce: “Five years after a community was forced to leave an encampment in Los Angeles’s Echo Park Lake, a team of archivists—including former residents—has preserved the memory of the encampment and the people who built a home there. The resulting exhibition, Tents and Tenants: After Echo Park Lake, is an online archive that collates artwork, photos, videos, and other memorabilia from the community.”

item.title: Archiving a Shuttered Japanese Drift Magazine’s Entire Back Catalog Is a Labor of Love
item.description: The Drive: “Despite the internet’s unreal utility in locating information, there’s still a lot out there in the world that you can’t find by pressing CTRL+F. So much knowledge, so much wisdom is stowed away in printed publications that will simply never be archived. JDM car dude Greg Mathews is making sure that can’t be said of Drift Tengoku, the first-ever magazine dedicated to driving sideways. He’s doing so by personally scanning and saving the pages from every issue he can get his hands on.”

item.title: Trump administration scraps meeting of high-profile tech panel
item.description: Reuters: “Technology shares sold off dramatically on Thursday on growing concerns that a new Congress controlled by Democrats will slow artificial intelligence development, and fears that the massive capital expenditure on building out AI will not yield sufficient returns. The market turmoil has heightened scrutiny of the sector among executives in Silicon Valley and policymakers in Washington.”

item.title: Elon Musk Deletes Election Posts After Republican Losses: His Own AI Helps Expose It
item.description: TechTimes: “Elon Musk has removed multiple election-related posts from his X account following a series of Republican defeats in the 2026 US midterm elections. The deletions came to light after users turned to Grok, the artificial intelligence chatbot developed by Musk’s xAI, to check whether the billionaire had been removing messages urging Americans to vote Republican.”

item.title: Online magazine Salon announces it is shutting down
item.description: Associated Press: “Salon, one of the early internet’s most influential websites that featured sharp voices and political and cultural journalism with a liberal sensibility, announced Thursday it would shut down after 31 years of publication. ‘It has been an extraordinary privilege,’ the outlet said in a farewell note.”

item.title: How WeRateDogs Is Fighting A.I. Slop, One Perfect Puppy at a Time
item.description: New York Times: “[Matt] Nelson’s company, WeRateDogs (Tagline: ‘your only source for professional dog rating’), is one of social media’s most successful dog-centric accounts, with some 20 million followers across X, Instagram, YouTube and TikTok. It has a thriving merchandise business, a podcast called ‘The Dogs Were Good (Again)’; and a charitable foundation that has raised nearly $5 million for needy dogs this year.”

item.title: Bluesky hit peak usage for the year on election night
item.description: TechCrunch: “COO Rose Wang told TechCrunch that usage began to peak between 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. PT, when many election results were rolling in. Daily posts and likes increased 30% and 70%, respectively, compared to the previous 30-day averages; clicks on links also spiked 20%.”

item.title: Researchers detect residential proxies on the White House network
item.description: This Week in Security: “In a blog post on Wednesday, network security company Layer3Intel said it discovered evidence of resproxies on the network run by the Executive Office of the President, or EOP, the office of top officials and staff in the president’s inner circle. The company said that it observed resproxy activity on the government network throughout October and into November. That means at least one device on the network allows outsiders to access the White House’s network.”

item.title: Meta, Google and TikTok sue California over teen online safety law
item.description: EdSource: “The law, Assembly Bill 1709, bans children younger than 16 from creating or keeping social media accounts on platforms that use ‘addictive features’ including algorithmic feeds. It requires social media companies to verify users’ age and delete existing accounts of those younger than 16 or face a civil penalty.”

item.title: Reno neon museum opens with nearly 50 historic signs
item.description: This Is Reno: “Nearly 50 historic neon signs and art pieces from Reno and across Nevada have found a home at the Light Circus Nevada Neon Museum, which opens to the public today, Oct. 30, at the downtown National Bowling Stadium. There was an opening ceremony Wednesday, which included lighting signs from former Reno landmarks including the Mapes Hotel, Nevada Club and Harolds Club.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: UCF Libraries Launches New Space Research Portal
item.description: University of Central Florida: “As America’s Space University, UCF has long been at the forefront of space-related research. Now, UCF Libraries is making it easier to discover and explore that work with the launch of the UCF Space Research Portal, a new online collection showcasing space-related scholarship produced by UCF researchers. Curated by UCF Libraries, the portal brings together published scholarly works across multiple disciplines including planetary science, aerospace engineering, astronomy, optics, and other fields connected to space exploration.”

item.title: Introducing The Third House, A Directory Of Connecticut Lobbyists
item.description: CTNewsJunkie: “The Third House is a searchable directory of the more than 1,500 lobbying registrations filed in Connecticut for the 2025-2026 term, showing every client and the firms and individual lobbyists working for them. It’s built from filings at the Office of State Ethics, updated as new filings come in, and includes a change log tracking who is entering and leaving the lobby.”

item.title: Rare museum photographs have been digitized in Mykolaiv
item.description: Intent: “A digital photo archive has been created in Mykolaiv, for which experts digitized 500 rare photographs and negatives from four local museums. The collection includes unique albums from the early 20th century, images of the Olbia excavations, and previously unknown portraits of the city’s prominent figures.”

item.title: Apple, Meta, Elon Musk’s companies reportedly in the crosshairs of congressional investigation
item.description: Mashable: “After a staggering Democratic sweep of the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some of those companies are preparing for what the Washington Post called an ‘investigative blitz’ in its report on the matter. According to the Post’s sources, which include congressional staffers, lawyers, and lobbyists, some of the targets of these investigations include Apple, Meta, and Elon Musk’s companies.”

item.title: Unhook lets you personalize the YouTube experience
item.description: MakeUseOf: “I use Chrome as my primary browser on my MacBook, and my experience with Unhook has been amazing. Unhook lets you remove algorithmic recommendations and distractions from YouTube’s user interface, so you can use YouTube for research, music, and entertainment without getting distracted. Unhook’s best feature is the sheer amount of customization options. The platform understands that everyone’s use is different and lets you design your experience.”

item.title: Google will fix Nest devices that didn’t adjust for Daylight Savings, breaking alarms and more
item.description: 9to5 Google: “Google says it will roll out a fix for Nest devices that were impacted by problems with Daylight Savings adjustments due to changes in Canada. A number of Nest Hub and Nest Thermostat users on Reddit noticed this week that their devices were showing the wrong time following the Daylight Savings time change.”

item.title: Latin America’s Catholic missionaries take to TikTok to reach younger generation
item.description: Reuters: “Catholic priests, nuns and deacons across Latin America are turning to social media to reach younger generations as church attendance and religious identity decline. The Vatican has embraced social media as a new evangelization frontier. During COVID-19 lockdowns, online religious ‌content surged and many sermons and celebrations moved online.”

item.title: Kona Historical Society is in jeopardy of closing; needs to raise $200,000 by Dec. 31
item.description: Big Island Now: “The Kona Historical Society should be celebrating its 50th birthday, but instead it is desperately trying to raise $200,000 by Dec. 31 to stay afloat. Laysan Unger, president of the board of directors for the Kona Historical Society, said the money is needed to remain open to the public, while providing the staff with the time and resources needed to reorganize, restructure and build a more sustainable future.”

item.title: Two killed, 20 injured in stampede at TikToker’s wedding event in Pakistan
item.description: Gulf News: “At least two people were killed and 20 injured in a stampede during a wedding celebration organised by a popular Pakistani TikToker in the city of Sialkot, Punjab province, after thousands of people reportedly gathered following promises of lavish prizes, according to media reports. The incident occurred at Faraz Sports Stadium ahead of a mehndi ceremony hosted by social media influencer Anser Mahmood, popularly known as Mr Patlo, who had invited members of the public to attend the celebrations.”

item.title: Greece Approves 10% Crypto Gains Tax Starting in 2027
item.description: Bitcoin Foundation: “Greece’s parliament has approved a 10% tax on cryptocurrency gains, per a Nov. 5 vote, with the Greece crypto tax framework set to begin Jan. 1, 2027. Annual net gains up to €500 are exempt. Staking, crypto lending and income from providing liquidity to decentralized protocols face a separate 15% levy.”

item.title: Nearly 500 cultural items repatriated by UK institutions over 12 years
item.description: University College London: “A new UCL-led study has produced the most comprehensive quantitative picture of cultural repatriation by UK heritage institutions, finding that 491 cultural items were returned between 2010 and 2022.”

item.title: The grammar of political hate? How a single word choice predicts nastier Facebook comment sections
item.description: PsyPost: “Subtle grammatical choices in political social media posts are linked to how much hostility users express in the comment sections below them. A large-scale analysis of Facebook discussions published in Social Psychological and Personality Science indicates that posts referring to political groups with nouns rather than adjectives, or making sweeping generalizations about a party, tend to attract a higher proportion of prejudiced replies. Although the effect of any single post is small, the findings suggest that everyday wording habits online could gradually contribute to political division.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Stylus celebrates as more than 30 years of music writing digitized
item.description: Winnipeg Free Press: “The Pompous Old Fart, the biting critiques of a young Bartley Kives, the formative years of the Weakerthans and Begonia … all captured in so many gonzo interviews and reviews. These hallmarks of Stylus Magazine will be celebrated at a party Thursday night at the West End Cultural Centre. The event marks the unveiling of the Stylus digital archive, which captures three-and-a-half decades of the back catalogue of Canada’s second-oldest independent music magazine, which was founded in 1989 as the program guide of what was then the University of Winnipeg’s in-house, closed-circuit radio station, CKUW (now CKUW 95.9 FM).”

item.title: Online archive under construction
item.description: e-flux: “Almost nine years of publishing, thousands of collaborations, and a new online infrastructure for Arts of the Working Class. Arts of the Working Class (AWC) soft introduces its new digital archive at artsoftheworkingclass.org, bringing together almost eight years of publishing on art, labor, poverty, and wealth.”

item.title: Merry Edwards Digital Collection Chronicles a Legendary Winemaker’s Career
item.description: UC Davis Library: “Scholars, journalists and wine lovers alike can now explore a selection of photographs, vintage release announcements, wine labels, production tasting notes and more that tell the story of a woman who broke into winemaking in the 1970s and helped pave the way for other women to enter the historically male-dominated industry. In addition to the sampling available online in the digital collection, additional materials from the Merry Edwards Papers are available by appointment from the library’s Archives and Special Collections.”

item.title: Exclusive-Google extends voluntary buyout offers to employees in several countries
item.description: Reuters: “Alphabet’s Google has expanded employee buyout offers to several countries this year as it looks to rein in rising costs amid heavy spending on artificial intelligence. The search engine company confirmed to Reuters that it began offering voluntary exit packages in June to some employees in Canada, France, Germany, Japan and Switzerland.”

item.title: Bluesky Gets a Midterms Bump, Ships Pronouns-in-Bios Feature
item.description: Gizmodo: “Bluesky is a calmer place to read posts than X for most users. It offers a much less infuriating algorithm, very little spam, and close to zero AI content if you don’t want to see any. Bluesky users mostly post about normal things—the majority of them apolitical. If someone acts like a troll there, they will at the very least get mass blocked. That absolutely makes the place more of a political bubble—and that’s something Schneider is concerned about—but it’s also part of the platform’s immune system and keeps things pleasant.”

item.title: Collins Dictionary chooses ‘mogging’ as its 2026 word of the year
item.description: Associated Press: “Collins Dictionary has named ‘mogging’ — a slang word meaning to outshine someone or something — as its word of the year. Dictionary experts said Tuesday that the word, most often used by young people ‘in a playful and ironic way when someone is upstaged,’ has entered mainstream language and saw a 210% increase in usage in 2026.”

item.title: Google is quietly hiding a new Zelda: Ocarina of Time Easter egg
item.description: Polygon: “The official release of the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is only a couple of days away, but search engine Google has already started the festivities with a clever nod to Nintendo’s landmark adventure game.”

item.title: Best Memes and TikToks After Midterms’ Blue Wave, From Regina George to ‘The Office’ References
item.description: Hollywood Reporter: “As conservatives grapple with what went wrong, liberals are reveling in their big wins, specifically with memes and TikTok flooding social media. Some people are even using clips from popular movies and TV shows — such as The Office, Avengers: Endgame, Breaking Bad, Mean Girls and Step Brothers — to express their euphoric feelings as well as take jabs at President Donald Trump, who is undoubtedly frustrated.”

item.title: Your computer can’t read a floppy disk – so how do we save the history they hold?
item.description: The Conversation: “Aging and outdated technology has rendered decades of data, memories and cultural heritage inaccessible and at risk of being lost. The constant churn of computer hardware and software upgrades means digital content from as little as 20 years ago cannot be accessed via today’s computers…. So much of our history is now stored on outmoded digital platforms. To help combat this, we recently worked with members of the Royal Historical Society of Victoria to archive their own materials. Here’s some of what we found.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Hungary: communist-era files released, up to 60,000 former agents revealed
item.description: Euronews: “Hungary released communist-era secret police files Wednesday, identifying up to 60,000 informants, a path for Hungary in reckoning with its repressive past. In spite of Hungary’s democratic transition in 1990, efforts to disclose communist-era archives have repeatedly failed, with critics blaming successive governments’ reluctance to implicate public figures across the political spectrum.”

item.title: National Songbook celebrates Australian music from Waltzing Matilda to The Presets
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “Banjo Paterson, The Presets and Yothu Yindi are among the first inductees enshrined in the National Songbook, an initiative that commemorates Australian music and the nation’s unofficial anthems. The National Film and Sound Archive of Australia (NSFA) and APRA AMCOS have joined forces to celebrate and preserve the songs and songwriters that helped shape Australia’s cultural identity.”

item.title: Tech barons cozied up to Trump. What will they do in newly blue America?
item.description: The Guardian: “Voters concerned about corruption expressed their displeasure at oligarchs’ blatant attempts to create a political environment to their liking. Voting against technocrats drove people into the hands of Democrats and away from Republicans. Tech oligarchs themselves, along with anger over the AI boom, datacenters and Flock surveillance cameras, shifted the tides.”

item.title: Elon Musk will face scrutiny from Democrats after midterms
item.description: NPR: “With a Democratic majority in Congress, the billionaire, who controls Tesla and SpaceX, will likely face investigations into the billions of dollars of government contracts his companies have been awarded since President Trump returned to office and his role leading the Department of Government Efficiency at the beginning of Trump’s second term.”

item.title: Snap shares fall over 10% on third-quarter revenue miss
item.description: CNBC: “Sales in Snap’s third quarter jumped 14% year-over-year while net income came in at $56 million, compared to the $104 million net loss it logged the prior year. Snap’s third-quarter adjusted earnings came in at $383 million, topping the $337 million that analysts were projecting, according to StreetAccount.”

item.title: Campaigns are investing in creators. What does that mean for voters?
item.description: Mashable: ” Creators are slipping voting reminders into beauty videos, candidates are sitting down with podcasters, and campaigns are paying online personalities to help reach voters. The 2026 midterms offer a look at how those relationships work in today’s influencer economy. Campaigns brief influencers on competitive races and collaborate on posts, while advocacy groups provide training, research, and financial support. Tonight, creators will also cover the midterms across YouTube livestreams alongside familiar network broadcasts.”

item.title: Trump’s $950 million presidential library on collision course with Democratic Congress
item.description: CBS News: “As President Trump prepares for the final two years of his presidency, he is expected to devote more attention to his presidential library, which has become a growing destination for money from companies and allies, according to current and former advisers who spoke on the condition of anonymity.”

item.title: Prominent Indian free speech groups say police ordered X accounts removed
item.description: Reuters: “Two of India’s most prominent digital rights and free speech groups said police in New Delhi have asked X ‌to remove their accounts, accusing them of defaming a Hindu nationalist ‌group linked to Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Free-speech activists and opposition politicians, including from India’s Congress party, ​say the move is a way to curb dissent in the world’s most populous nation.”

item.title: Ukraine’s drone strikes spur hasty Russian plans for underground data centers
item.description: Ars Technica: “Russian tech companies are scrambling to harden and hide their data centers underground after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged facilities housing AI supercomputers and disrupted cloud services for millions of Russian users. Meanwhile, the Kremlin is requiring data center owners to reserve computing capacity for emergency state needs and has even authorized possible use of foreign data centers.”

item.title: Japanese Arcade Machines Have Been Taken Down By A Major Hack Of Sega’s Services
item.description: Kotaku: “The online services of a number of Japanese arcade games, including heavy hitters such as Bandai Namco’s Taiko no Tatsujin and Sega’s Initial D: The Arcade, have been forced offline due to a widespread hack of online services ALL.net and Aime. As of November 1st at 3 p.m. local time in Japan, all services involving these networks have been affected, while Sega Fave—the Sega subsidiary in charge of the service—investigates the breach.”

item.title: BLM Launches Map Identifying Helium Concentrations on Public Lands
item.description: Bureau of Land Management: “The Bureau of Land Management has launched a publicly available web-based GIS mapping tool to help promote helium development and production on public lands. The interactive tool highlights areas on BLM-managed lands with helium concentrations.”

item.title: Google researchers demand freedom to tell the world what they know about AI
item.description: Washington Post: This article is syndicated on MSN and has no paywall. “Workers inside Google’s artificial intelligence division are pushing executives to release them from non-disparagement agreements, arguing that they must be free to inform the public about the risks of the technology they are working to advance, according to sources inside the company.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Midterm Voters Reject Data Centers
item.description: Washington Sun: “It was a bad night for data centers. In hotly contested gubernatorial races, Democrats who campaigned on pausing development beat Republican challengers who proposed more moderate approaches. At least 38 towns and cities passed ballot measures to restrict data centers locally.”

item.title: Plans for a data center threaten scenic wilderness and dark skies in West Virginia
item.description: NPR: “Those inky-black nights — and the natural beauty they shelter — are now under threat from what many residents see as a modern-day version of extractive industries like logging and mining that once defined the region. In a place where tourism, outdoor recreation and community are deeply intertwined, a gigantic power plant and data center campus in nearby Tucker County would bring large-scale development into the heart of it all.”

item.title: ‘Elonville’: US residents say Musk’s xAI offered to buy homes if they don’t sue over datacenter noise
item.description: The Guardian: “Real estate agents have been going door to door in Southaven, Mississippi, on behalf of xAI, touting a deal to purchase houses as long as the owners agree to not join a lawsuit against the company over the power plant’s noise. (Musk’s AI company officially became SpaceXAI in July and has lately been rebranded as SpaceXSI but to neighbors of the datacenter in Mississippi, it remains xAI.)”

item.title: Finnish police launch criminal probe over forest cleared for Google data center
item.description: The Hill: “Finnish police opened a criminal investigation Thursday into Google’s work on a planned data center in northern Finland after the company cleared hundreds of acres of forest without completing required environmental reviews.”

item.title: Fashion’s AI era: face swaps and digital clones
item.description: Reuters: “AI-generated fashion models present a tantalizing opportunity for brands: the ability to create lifelike images for their retail websites while cutting costs by 90% or more compared to photo shoots with human models. For the modeling industry, the technology poses an existential threat because of scant regulation governing the ownership or use of digital twins.”

item.title: Fort Bend County Judge Daniel Wong faces backlash over AI-generated video of Black voters
item.description: Houston Public Media: “The Republican candidate for Fort Bend County Judge is facing backlash after his campaign shared an AI-generated video on social media, appearing to show Black voters expressing their support because he helped them pay their bills and find jobs.”

item.title: Trump tried to rebrand “AI” as “SI.” Right-wing outlets aren’t listening.
item.description: Media Matters: “President Donald Trump appears to have finally found a hoop through which his right-wing media sycophants won’t jump. A month after he demanded that the public adopt his preferred terms “SI” and ‘super intelligence,’ outlets including Fox News, Newsmax, and even Breitbart continue to use ‘artificial intelligence’ and ‘AI.'”

item.title: Reactions: Princeton is buying us ChatGPT subscriptions
item.description: Daily Princetonian: “On Wednesday, Princeton announced that it will provide free access to ChatGPT for students, faculty, and staff starting next semester, a change that has drawn mixed reactions across campus. Our Opinion editors and staff share their reactions to the announcement and its implications amid ongoing conversations about AI use in the classroom.”

item.title: As the US and China form AI blocs, countries are increasingly torn between them
item.description: Associated Press: “With the two leading AI powers, the United States and China, forming their own AI blocs, other countries are maneuvering to harness the strengths of both groupings and avoid losing out.”

item.title: The Making of Dario Amodei
item.description: New York Times: “Some call him a doomer. Others see him as a responsible technologist. Here’s how the Anthropic chief executive’s thinking on artificial intelligence was shaped.”

item.title: Anthropic Strikes Its First Licensing Deal, With the AP, for Election Coverage
item.description: AdWeek: “If, by chance, you opened Claude on Election Night and asked it for an update on the latest polling data, you would have been treated to a novel sight: up-the-minute information, provided by and attributed to the Associated Press. This new development was the result of a content and data licensing deal struck between the two organizations, which was struck just before the midterm elections, according to two people familiar with the matter.”

item.title: New York Times and other outlets sue web browser Brave over alleged content scraping
item.description: TechCrunch: “The New York Times sued Brave, the 11-year-old, privacy-focused browser company, on Monday, alleging it scraped the outlet’s copyrighted content and unlawfully distributed it to customers the suit names as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere. Separately on Monday, the Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel filed a similar lawsuit. Both were brought in federal court in Manhattan.”

item.title: Turkish watchdog opens probe into Google’s AI-generated summaries
item.description: Hurriyet Daily News: “Türkiye’s Competition Authority launched an investigation into Google’s artificial intelligence services on Nov. 2, citing concerns that AI-generated summaries and overviews could be reducing traffic to news websites. The investigation targeted Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode services, with the body ordering interim measures, according to a written statement by the board.”

item.title: IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant
item.description: IEEE Spectrum: “IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite, built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards, journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more.”

item.title: AI models cost more when you don’t use English
item.description: Rest of World: “People who use less widely spoken languages could end up paying more to use artificial intelligence than those who speak English or other dominant languages. A new study published last month by the Coalition for Language Equity in AI Research found AI models require far more tokens for some languages than others.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Howard Student’s Database Spotlights Missing And Murdered Black Women In D.C.
item.description: Howard University News Service: “[Avery] Bernard Johns designed DEADLINING, a database that centralizes information on cases of missing and murdered Black women and girls in the D.C. area. ‘This could just be publicly available information, but no one in the government is doing it,’ Bernard Johns said. ‘I knew that I could do it, so I taught myself how to code.’ In addition to its searchable database, DEADLINING offers an interactive map and geospatial analysis that the D.C. Missing Persons website does not.”

item.title: Weaving ‘Tapestries’: Introducing A New Tool for Digital Storytelling and Archiving
item.description: Internet Archive Blog: “Tapestries is a user interface developed by Bob Stein and Dan Visel (who works on the Wayback team) that allows people to make dynamic, multi-linear presentations with various digital objects. The curation tool lets users gather items from all over the web and put them together into a single space to tell a story. Rather than simply listing links at the end of a document, a tapestry can be designed by dragging photos, video clips or other items onto a digital canvas that viewers can click to open.”

item.title: Google turns off AI for schoolchildren by default
item.description: AFP: “Google has said it will switch off its AI tools for schoolchildren by default, after drawing criticism for pushing artificial intelligence features to students while schools are still debating how the technology should be used in classrooms.”

item.title: Elon Musk suffers major blow in US midterms
item.description: Politico: “He doled out around $446 million — the most a non-candidate has ever spent on an election, including over $200 million on Texas-related efforts. Musk’s preferred candidates across the country were swamped, losing almost everywhere, including Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race and Vivek Ramaswamy in the Ohio gubernatorial race.”

item.title: ‘The Last Jedi’ Director Launches a New Camera App for iPhone (Because He’s a Good Guy)
item.description: Gizmodo: “[Rian] Johnson announced the new app Wednesday in a post on X. “So I recently badgered my cinematographer [Steve Yedlin] into making my ideal iPhone still camera app. It shoots RAW, bypasses the iPhone’s look processing and instead uses the same image processing we use on our movies,” Johnson wrote in the post.”

item.title: This bike will stop your kid’s YouTube video if they’re not pedaling
item.description: Tubefilter: “The reason Tovie piqued our interest is Dalmia and Jain’s proprietary ‘Pedal-to-Play’ system, which ‘makes movement the controller,’ they say. It works by connecting Tovie to a kid’s device via Bluetooth, and whenever they stop pedaling, the YouTube video they’re watching (or the video game they’re playing) stops working. The goal is to keep kids moving their bodies but still allowing them screen time.”

item.title: GSA left sensitive Google Drive files open to staff, contractors
item.description: The Register: “The General Services Administration (GSA), which handles contracting, procurement, property management, and other elements of basic operations for federal agencies, has faced repeated findings of inadequate protection for controlled unclassified information (CUI) since at least 2014, according to a report from the agency’s Office of Inspector General. Again.”

item.title: Google shuts down a sneaky malware backdoor on millions of Android TV and Google TV boxes
item.description: 9to5 Google: “Google has confirmed that an Android TV device maker snuck a backdoor for malware onto certified devices, which is leading to security improvements for the ecosystem as a whole. In a post today, Google confirmed that it has cut ties with ‘Videostrong,’ a company that was manufacturing certified Android TV boxes.”

item.title: Karl Bushby embraces emotional mother as he completes his 28-year, 31,000-mile walk around world
item.description: Associated Press: “Karl Bushby embraced his weeping mother in his arms Monday as he returned to his northern England home to complete a 28-year odyssey to walk around the world. ‘Where have you been?’ his mother, Angela, asked as he arrived outside the home he left in 1998 that was now decked with a banner saying ‘Welcome Home Son.’ He didn’t need to tell her.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: ElectionsArchive.com
item.description: Found in my Calishat Snaps: , currently in beta. From the About page: “Elections Archive is a free archive of election results, from each country’s first elections to its latest, down to the finest unit the official count reports. The archive covers ten countries and the European Union: the United States, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Canada, Türkiye, Italy, Germany, France, Ireland, and Brazil. It goes back to 1787 in the United States, 1832 in the United Kingdom, and 1848 in Switzerland, and down to precincts, polling stations, and ballot boxes where the official count goes that deep.”

item.title: Digitizing Virginia’s “Free Negro Registers”
item.description: Library of Virginia: “They said it couldn’t be done—that tracking down, borrowing, and digitizing every surviving ‘Free Negro Register’ in Virginia was simply too massive a project to pull off…. Thanks to dedicated efforts of many Library of Virginia archivists and digital librarians, the generosity of several genealogists and cultural heritage professionals, and participation of Virginia circuit court clerks and records room archivists, there are now ninety-nine register books representing sixty different Virginia localities available through the Library of Virginia’s digital collections.”

item.title: Search More Than 500 Cases of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
item.description: ProPublica: “We have tallied and cataloged every case we can find of an immigration agent reportedly detaining a citizen during the current administration — more than 500 cases from Inauguration Day through Oct. 21, 2026.”

item.title: New Database Mapping Foreign Nationals across Regions of Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary and Poland
item.description: Institute of Economic Research SAS: “The Institute of Economic Research of the Slovak Academy of Sciences, in cooperation with partners from Mendel University in Brno, the University of Łódź, and the Kopint Foundation for Economic Research in Budapest, has published the Central Europe Migration Database (CEMD) – a database that harmonises data on foreign nationals from national registers in Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, and Poland into a single comparable structure.”

item.title: Congress Corral Offline Until Next Year
item.description: Calishat: “As the elections are underway, I have taken down CongressCorral.com with the idea of relaunching it with the new class of legislators in early 2025. I will probably do some other upgrades as well.”

item.title: Getty Launches Global Initiative to Advance Museum Interpretation Practices
item.description: Getty: “Getty announced today the launch of ‘New Interpretations,’ a grant initiative to strengthen visitor-centered approaches to the interpretation of artwork at museums worldwide. For its pilot round of grants, Getty has awarded $2.7 million for 11 projects at museums and arts organizations that will prioritize and deepen connections between audiences and artworks.”

item.title: It’s harder than ever to spot fake content online. Here are some strategies.
item.description: Mashable: “It’s online where you’ll be lulled into doomscrolling, engage in unhealthy digital interactions, or witness violence. A good portion of what you see may not even be real. It may be trying to intentionally deceive you. For those staying online, there is at least one way to protect yourself from false information: Stop and ask why.”

item.title: Woman swatted by scammer after she refused to follow instructions: police
item.description: WKRC: “Authorities said a woman was swatted by a scammer after she refused to comply with demands. Police are investigating a swatting incident linked to a fraud attempt, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said in a statement.”

item.title: Lafayette activist sues U.S. Rep. Higgins over Facebook blocking
item.description: The Current (Louisiana): “Lafayette community activist Matthew Humphrey is suing U.S. Rep. Clay Higgins, alleging the congressman violated his First Amendment rights by blocking him two years ago from his official Facebook page in retaliation for political criticism.”

item.title: A new report accuses Microsoft of using 10 “dark patterns” to keep you on Edge
item.description: TechSpot: “It’s no secret that when it comes to pushing its Edge browser onto users, Microsoft isn’t afraid to play dirty. There have been numerous stories about the aggressive tactics the company uses, and other browser makers aren’t happy about it. Now, a new report dives into the ‘dark patterns’ Microsoft adopts to get more people onto Edge.”

item.title: A humble Excel spreadsheet gives rise to a massive online database of Hittite
item.description: UCLA: “While conducting research on Hittite in 2023, Anthony Yates began cataloging the language’s linguistic features on an Excel spreadsheet…. But as Yates’ simple spreadsheet grew, he realized he could turn it into a resource that would be useful for other scholars. So, supported by grants from UCLA DataX and the UCLA Jeffrey P. Cunard Center for Global Antiquity, Yates and a small team of students are transforming his Excel document into an interactive database called the Morphologically and Phonologically Annotated Database of Hittite.”

item.title: How to prepare your online life for your death
item.description: The Conversation: “We studied challenges older adults encounter when thinking about what should happen to their online accounts after they die. We interviewed 21 American adults over age 60 to learn about their concerns, needs and practices for their online accounts, as well as what would make planning for these accounts easier.” Good morning, Internet…
